match.reason: The closest bank point, Young's double slit, covers the fringe pattern and in-phase and out-of-phase interference, but it never teaches the path-difference condition itself (whole wavelengths for bright, half wavelengths for dark), so it is broader and related rather than the same idea.

draft.title: Path difference and interference
card: Path difference is the difference in the distances travelled by two waves from their sources to the same point. It is measured in wavelengths (λ).
if the path difference is 0, λ, 2λ and so on (nλ), the waves arrive in phase. Crests meet crests, so the light is bright.
if the path difference is ½λ, 1½λ, 2½λ and so on ((n + ½)λ), the waves arrive out of phase. Crests meet troughs, so the light is dark.

This works when the two sources are coherent, meaning they have the same wavelength and a fixed phase relationship. In a double slit pattern, the centre of the screen is equally far from both slits, so its path difference is 0 and it is bright.
draft.remember: Path difference of a whole number of wavelengths gives bright. A half-wavelength offset gives dark.

a.q: Light from two coherent sources reaches a point on a screen. One path is 3.0 wavelengths longer than the other. What is seen at that point?
opts: A bright band, as the waves arrive in phase
A dark band, as the waves arrive out of phase
A dark band, as the path difference is an odd number
A bright band, as the waves cancel each other out
a.why: A path difference of 3λ is a whole number of wavelengths, so crests meet crests and the light is bright. A dark band needs a half-wavelength offset such as 2.5λ or 3.5λ, not a whole number.
a.clue: Is 3.0 a whole number of wavelengths or a half-way value?

b.q: In a double slit setup, a point P on the screen is 2.5 wavelengths further from slit 1 than from slit 2. A point Q is 2.0 wavelengths further from slit 1 than from slit 2. What is seen at P and Q?
opts: P is dark and Q is bright
P is bright and Q is dark
P and Q are both bright
P and Q are both dark
b.why: At P the path difference is 2.5λ, a half-wavelength offset, so the waves arrive out of phase and P is dark. At Q it is 2.0λ, a whole number, so Q is bright. Taking 2.5 as the larger number does not make P brighter.
b.clue: Check which path difference is a whole number and which ends in a half.

a.best: A bright band, as the waves arrive in phase

b.best: P is dark and Q is bright

problems.detail: The card says path difference 'is measured in wavelengths (λ)'. Path difference is a distance, measured in metres, that is often expressed as a multiple of λ. As written, students may think wavelengths are its unit.

Coherence is defined as 'a fixed phase relationship', but the rules nλ = bright and (n + ½)λ = dark, and the bright centre, only hold when the sources are in phase. Coherent sources with a constant non-zero phase difference would shift the pattern. The card should say the sources are in phase, as in a double slit lit by one source.

check.summary: Both questions are correct with one clear answer each. The card blurs path difference (a distance in metres) with its expression in wavelengths, and it does not say the bright/dark rules assume the sources are in phase, not just coherent.
